title: Game Leaderboard
prompt: Design a live leaderboard for an online game with tens of millions of players: show the top players and tell any player their exact rank right after a match.

clarify.q: Does a player's leaderboard score come from their best match or the sum of all matches?
clarify.why: Best score means 'update only if higher' (ZADD GT); a running total means an increment (ZINCRBY). They behave differently on retries: a repeated increment double-counts, a repeated 'max' does not.

clarify.q: How many players are ranked, and does every player need an exact rank?
clarify.why: Exact rank for 50 M players is cheap in one sorted set. Exact rank for 1 B players across shards is expensive, and 'top 12%' might be good enough below the top 10 000.
Either 'whoever got there first ranks higher' (needs a timestamp folded into the score) or 'tied players share a rank' (needs a count of strictly higher scores). This changes the score encoding.

clarify.q: Are there seasons, and what happens when one ends?
clarify.why: Seasons mean a fresh board per season, a freeze at the cutoff, and a durable snapshot for rewards. They also bound the board's size and the timestamp range.

clarify.q: Who reports scores: the game client or a game server?
clarify.why: Client-reported scores are trivially faked. If a trusted match server reports results, the leaderboard can treat them as truth and focus on idempotency.

clarify.q: Do we need friend leaderboards or regional boards too?
clarify.why: Each extra board multiplies writes. Friend boards are usually computed on read from the global scores instead of stored per player.

clarify.q: How fresh must ranks be after a match?
clarify.why: Within a second or two lets us update the board asynchronously from the score database. Instant read-your-write for the player can be handled on the client.

functional: After a match, a player's season score is updated and visible on the board within 2 s.
Anyone can view the top 100 players for the current season.
A player can see their exact rank and score, plus the 5 players just above and below them.
Ties are broken by who reached the score first.
Each season has its own board; final standings are frozen and kept for rewards.
nonFunctional: Rank and top-100 queries p99 under 50 ms.
Handle ~6 k score updates/s and ~12 k reads/s at peak.
No lost or double-counted match results: scores in the board must match the score database.
The board can be rebuilt from the database in under 10 minutes if the cache is lost.
99.9% availability for reads; the game must keep working if the leaderboard is degraded.
outOfScope: Reward delivery after the season (we only produce the final standings)

assumptions: 50 M players ranked per season, 10 M daily active
Each active player finishes 10 matches a day
Each active player opens the leaderboard 20 times a day
Peak (evening, event weekends) is 5× the daily average

steps.label: Sorted set memory
steps.math: 50 M members × ~120 B (skiplist node, hash entry, 16 B member id, 8 B score)
steps.result: ≈ 6 GB: fits one Redis node with room to spare

steps.label: Cost of one update or rank query
Load on one Redis node
steps.math: 6 k + 12 k = 18 k ops/s against ~100 k simple ops/s per node
steps.result: ≈ 20% of one node at peak; a replica covers failover

steps.label: Rebuild from database
steps.math: 50 M ZADDs pipelined at ~200 k/s = 250 s

estimates.takeaway: At 50 M players this is a one-node problem: a single Redis sorted set of about 6 GB answers every query in logarithmic time with headroom to spare. The design effort goes into correctness (ties, idempotent updates, seasons, rebuild) rather than distribution. Sharding becomes necessary only at roughly 10× players or if one node's write rate becomes the limit, and every sharding scheme makes 'what is my exact rank' more expensive.

api.body: { matchId, seasonId, results: [{ playerId, score }], endedAt }
api.note: Called by the trusted game server, never the client. matchId is the idempotency key: repeats are ignored.

api.returns: 200 { entries: [{ rank, playerId, name, score }], asOf }
api.note: Cached for 1 s at the API layer, so thousands of viewers share one Redis call.

api.returns: 200 { rank, score, around: [{ rank, playerId, score }] }
api.note: One ZREVRANK plus one ZREVRANGE from max(0, rank−5) to rank+5.
Fetch friends' scores in one ZMSCORE call and sort them in the service; no stored per-friend board.

entities.name: MatchResult
entities.why: Raw facts. The primary key makes replays of the same match a no-op.

entities.name: SeasonScore
entities.store: Postgres, same shard as the player
entities.why: The durable truth the board is built from; used for rebuilds and for the final season snapshot.

entities.name: Board
entities.why: Keeps members ordered by score with O(log n) insert, rank and range queries.

entities.name: SeasonStanding
entities.store: Postgres or columnar files in object storage
entities.why: Frozen final standings for rewards and history; written once at season end.

data.note: The database is the source of truth and Redis is a derived view that can be thrown away and rebuilt. A score change updates SeasonScore and writes an outbox row in the same transaction; a relay applies it to Redis. This keeps the two consistent without distributed transactions. The board key includes the season, so a new season simply starts a new key, and the old key is deleted after its snapshot is written.

hld.summary:
Game servers post match results to the score service. It writes MatchResult and updates SeasonScore in Postgres, adding an outbox row in the same transaction. An outbox relay reads new rows and applies them to the Redis sorted set for the season, using a conditional update so stale or repeated events cannot lower a score.

The leaderboard API answers reads straight from Redis replicas. The top-100 list is cached in process for one second because everyone asks the same question. At season end a season job freezes the board, writes final standings to durable storage and opens the next season's key.

diagram.title: Score write path and leaderboard read path
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  GS[Game servers] --> SS[Score service]
  SS --> PG[(Postgres scores and outbox)]
  PG --> RL[Outbox relay]
  RL --> RP[(Redis primary sorted set)]
  RP --> RR[(Redis replicas)]
  P[Player app] --> API[Leaderboard API]
  API --> TC[Top 100 cache 1 s]
  API --> RR
  SJ[Season job] --> RP
  SJ --> ST[(Season standings)]

flows.title: A match finishes
steps: Game server posts { matchId, results } once the match ends.
Score service inserts MatchResult rows; a duplicate matchId hits the primary key and is ignored.
For each player, it updates SeasonScore if the new score is higher and writes an outbox row in the same transaction.
The relay applies ZADD lb:{season} GT encodedScore playerId to Redis within about a second.
The player's client already shows their own new score optimistically; the next rank query confirms it.

flows.title: A player checks their rank
steps: API runs ZREVRANK lb:{season} playerId on a replica and gets rank r (0-based).
It runs ZREVRANGE lb:{season} max(0, r−5) r+5 WITHSCORES to get neighbours (clamped, because a negative index in Redis counts from the bottom of the set).
It decodes the scores and returns rank r+1 with the 11 rows.

flows.title: The season ends
steps: At the cutoff, new results are written with the next season's id; results for matches that started before the cutoff still count for the old season for 10 minutes.
After the grace period, the season job reads SeasonScore ordered by score and achievedAt and writes SeasonStanding.
It checks the top 1 000 against the Redis board and alerts on any difference.
The old Redis key is deleted a day later.

deepDives.title: Where ranks come from: SQL, a sorted set, or score buckets
deepDives.problem: 'Top 100' is easy almost anywhere. 'What is my rank among 50 M' is the hard query. In a relational database it means counting how many players have a higher score. A B-tree index on score can find the player fast but does not store subtree counts, so the count walks every index entry above them: about 25 M entries for a median player. At 12 k reads/s that is not workable.

options.name: Relational table with an index on score
options.how: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM season_score WHERE score > :mine; top N with ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 100.
pros: Strong consistency and durability for free
No extra system
cons: Rank cost grows with rank: millions of index entries per query for mid-ranked players
Heavy reads compete with score writes

options.name: Redis sorted set
options.how: A skiplist plus hash table keeps members ordered by score. ZADD, ZREVRANK and ZREVRANGE are all O(log n).
pros: Exact rank in microseconds at 50 M members
Simple commands for top N, my rank and neighbours
Single-threaded execution makes each command atomic
cons: In memory: about 6 GB here, 60 GB at 10×
Not a durable source of truth; needs a rebuild path
One node's CPU caps write throughput

options.name: Score buckets (histogram)
options.how: Keep a count of players per score bucket (for example 10 000 buckets). Rank ≈ sum of counts of higher buckets plus a position inside the bucket.
pros: Tiny memory; easy to shard and merge
Constant-time percentile for any player
cons: Only approximate inside a bucket
Exact top-N still needs a separate sorted structure

deepDives.choice: A Redis sorted set for the whole season, with Postgres as the source of truth. At 50 M players it fits easily on one node and answers all three queries exactly. I would keep a histogram as a cheap add-on for showing percentiles ('top 8%') on profile pages. I would drop Redis and stay in SQL only for a small game (under a few hundred thousand players), where the count scan is short enough and one less system is worth more.

deepDives.title: Ties and encoding the score
deepDives.problem: Players often have the same score, especially near round numbers. Redis orders equal scores by the member string, which here means by player ID: arbitrary and unfair. We want 'reached it first ranks higher'. Redis scores are 64-bit doubles, which hold integers exactly only up to 2^53, so any packing scheme must stay inside 53 bits.

options.name: Pack score and time into one number
options.how: encoded = score × 2^23 + (2^23 − 1 − secondsSinceSeasonStart). A 90-day season is 7 776 000 s, under 2^23 = 8 388 608. Scores up to 2^20 (about 1 M) leave the total at 43 bits.
pros: One sorted set, one command per query
Earlier achievers get a larger tail and rank higher among equals
cons: Caps score range and season length; must be designed up front
Every reader must decode the number

options.name: Shared rank for ties
options.how: Store the raw score; rank = 1 + ZCOUNT(lb, '(' + score, '+inf'), the count of strictly higher scores.
pros: Fair when the game has no notion of 'first'
No encoding
cons: Two commands per rank query
Order among tied players on the top-100 page is still arbitrary

options.name: Secondary sort in the database
options.how: Use Redis only to find the score; resolve ties by querying achievedAt in SQL.
pros: No precision limits
cons: Extra database read on hot paths
Hard to do for neighbour lists

deepDives.choice: Pack score and time into one double. 20 bits of score plus 23 bits of time is 43 bits, safely inside the 53-bit exact range, and a single ZREVRANK is still enough. Use seconds since season start, not epoch time, to keep the field small. Store achievedAt in Postgres too, so a rebuild produces the same encoding. If the game's scores could exceed about 1 M, I would give score more bits and time fewer (minutes instead of seconds needs only 17 bits for 90 days). If the product prefers shared ranks, switch to the ZCOUNT approach.

deepDives.title: Sharding a leaderboard
deepDives.problem: At 500 M players the set is ~60 GB and peak writes approach 60 k/s, which is uncomfortable for one Redis node. But splitting a sorted set breaks the property that made it useful: no single node knows a player's global rank anymore. Each sharding scheme makes a different query expensive.

options.name: Hash players across k shards
options.how: Shard by hash(playerId). Top N: ask every shard for its top N and merge. My rank: sum, over all shards, the count of members with a higher score (ZCOUNT).
pros: Even load and memory regardless of score distribution
A player stays on one shard all season
cons: Every rank query hits all k shards (k round trips, slowest shard sets latency)
Top N reads k × N entries

options.name: Partition by score range
options.how: Shard 1 holds the highest scores, shard 2 the next band, and so on. Keep a small table of member counts per shard. Rank = counts of all higher shards + local rank.
pros: Rank needs one shard plus a cached count table
Top N reads only the top shard
cons: Score distribution is skewed and drifts during a season, so bands need rebalancing
A player whose score crosses a band must be removed from one shard and added to another, which is not atomic
The top shard gets the most read traffic

options.name: Exact top tier, approximate tail
options.how: Keep exact sorted sets only for players above a threshold (for example top 100 k); everyone else gets a bucket-based percentile from a histogram that shards and merges easily.
pros: Small exact set; histogram is tiny and easy to scale
Matches what players care about: nobody needs rank 31 402 117 exactly
cons: The product must accept 'top 23%' instead of an exact rank for most players
Players near the threshold need care when crossing it

deepDives.choice: For the stated 50 M players: don't shard, run one primary and replicas. If we grow 10×, I would pick exact top tier plus approximate tail, because it keeps the most-viewed queries exact and cheap and turns the long tail into a trivial counting problem. If the product insists on exact ranks for everyone, choose hash sharding with parallel ZCOUNTs: with 8 shards that is 8 small calls in parallel, around a few milliseconds, and it never needs rebalancing. Score-range sharding looks clever but its rebalancing and cross-band moves make it the most fragile choice.

diagram.title: My rank with hash-sharded boards
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Leaderboard API
  participant S1 as Shard 1
  participant S2 as Shard 2
  participant S3 as Shard 3
  A->>S2: ZSCORE for player on home shard
  S2-->>A: encoded score
  par count higher on each shard
    A->>S1: ZCOUNT above score
    A->>S2: ZCOUNT above score
    A->>S3: ZCOUNT above score
  end
  S1-->>A: 1200
  S2-->>A: 1180
  S3-->>A: 1215
  Note over A: rank is 3595 plus 1 equals 3596

deepDives.title: Keeping the board consistent with the database
deepDives.problem: The board must equal the scores in the database, yet updates arrive by many paths: retries from game servers, relay restarts, out-of-order delivery, and full rebuilds. A naive 'write DB, then write Redis' in the request can lose the Redis write if the process dies between the two, and a replayed increment can double-count.

options.name: Dual write in the request
options.how: Score service writes Postgres and then Redis in the same request handler.
pros: Lowest latency
Simple to read
cons: A crash between the two writes leaves Redis behind forever
Retries can double-apply increments

options.name: Outbox relay with idempotent updates
options.how: Write SeasonScore and an outbox row in one transaction; a relay applies outbox rows to Redis with ZADD GT (only raise) and marks them done.
pros: No lost updates: the outbox row survives crashes
ZADD GT makes replays and reordering harmless for best-score boards
cons: Adds about a second of lag
Relay must be monitored for backlog

options.name: Redis as the only store, with persistence
options.how: Skip the database; rely on Redis AOF and replicas for durability.
pros: Fewest moving parts
cons: Fsync settings trade throughput for loss on crash
Season rewards depend on data that was never in a durable, queryable store

deepDives.choice: Outbox relay with idempotent updates. For a best-score board, ZADD with the GT flag means applying the same or an older event again never lowers a score, so at-least-once delivery is safe. For a cumulative board, the relay must dedupe by matchId (a Redis set of applied match IDs per season with a TTL), because increments are not idempotent. A nightly job compares a sample of players in Redis against Postgres and alerts on drift. If the board must reflect the player's own score instantly, the client shows it optimistically; nobody else notices a one-second lag.

failures: Promote a replica (a few seconds of failed writes, retried from the outbox). Reads continue from the remaining replicas. Writes acknowledged by the old primary but not replicated are re-applied from the outbox.
Rebuild from SeasonScore with pipelined ZADDs in about 4 minutes. Serve the top-100 from the last cached copy and show 'ranks updating' meanwhile.
The outbox relay falls behind during a tournament
Ranks lag but nothing is lost. Alert on backlog age over 10 s, scale relays by partitioning the outbox by player ID.
A bug lets a cheated score of 2 billion through
Validate scores against the game's maximum at the score service. Remove the player with ZREM and fix SeasonScore; the encoded format also rejects values above 2^20.
The top-100 page gets a traffic spike when a stream mentions it
The 1 s in-process cache means each API instance makes at most one Redis call per second for it, regardless of viewers.
scale: 10× players (500 M): ~60 GB and ~60 k writes/s peak. Move to an exact top tier plus histogram tail, or hash-shard with parallel ZCOUNTs if exact ranks are required.
Many boards (regional, weekly, per mode): each is its own key; place keys on different Redis nodes by hashing the board key so no node hosts all the hot boards.
Global players: keep one writable board region; serve reads from replicas in other regions with sub-second lag.
Historical queries: past seasons are read from SeasonStanding in the database or columnar files, never kept in Redis.

followups.q: How do you build a friends leaderboard?
answer: Fetch the player's friend IDs (say up to 500) and call ZMSCORE once for all of them.
Sort the 500 scores in the service; that costs microseconds.
Cache the result for a few seconds per player; there is no need to store a board per player.

followups.q: How would a daily or weekly board work alongside the season board?
answer: Use separate keys such as lb:daily:2026-11-02 and write to each from the relay.
Set a TTL so old daily boards expire automatically after their snapshot is written.
Each extra board adds one write per score update, so keep the number of boards small or compute rare ones from the database.

followups.q: Why not let the game client report scores?
answer: Anyone can call the API with a fake score; leaderboards are the first thing cheaters attack.
Have the authoritative match server report results, signed with a service credential.
Add sanity checks: maximum plausible score, score per minute played, and review flags for sudden jumps.

followups.q: How do you show ranks like 'you moved up 340 places'?
answer: Return the previous rank stored in the client from the last visit, or store last-seen rank per player.
Compute the difference on read; it is a display feature, not part of the board.

followups.q: What if two matches for the same player finish at the same time?
answer: For best-score boards, ZADD GT is atomic in Redis, so whichever is higher wins regardless of order.
In Postgres, use UPDATE ... SET bestScore = GREATEST(bestScore, :new) so the database agrees.
For cumulative boards, both increments apply exactly once because each is deduped by matchId.

mistakes: Computing rank with COUNT(*) over a SQL table at thousands of reads per second.
Treating Redis as the only copy of scores with no rebuild path.
Ignoring ties, so equal scores are ordered by player ID.
Sharding a 6 GB sorted set across many nodes before the numbers require it.

mid: Estimated write and read rates and the sorted set's memory, and concluded one node is enough
Used a sorted set with ZADD, ZREVRANK and ZREVRANGE for top N, my rank and neighbours
Asked how ties are broken and handled them explicitly
Kept a durable database as the source of truth with a rebuild path
senior: Explained why SQL rank queries get slower with rank (counting index entries)
Encoded score and time into one double and checked it fits in 53 bits
Made updates idempotent (ZADD GT or matchId dedupe) and propagated them via an outbox
Described season end: grace period, freeze, durable snapshot, verification
Cached the shared top-100 response to absorb read spikes
staff: Compared hash sharding, score-range sharding and exact-top plus approximate-tail, naming which query each makes expensive
Argued from the numbers that sharding is not needed yet and named the trigger for it
Covered score integrity: server-authoritative results and sanity limits
Planned drift detection between Redis and the database
